KEY MESSAGE 1...A cold front moves through the region tonight 
bringing some rain. 

A cold front will move south and eastward through the area this
evening into the overnight bringing some rain/showers with it. A
few rumbles of thunder are not out of the question either. There's
not much instability to work with but PWATs are quite high at 
around 2 inches. Also, there are some upstream reports towards 
central PA of a quick .50 to 1.0 inches of rain with these 
showers as they've moved through. Generally not expecting any 
issues but if the line of showers currently moving through were 
to slow down and train near the urban corridor that could result
in some localized flooding issues this evening. Expect showers 
to wind down overnight as the front continues to push south. 

KEY MESSAGE 2...A frontal boundary south of the region will 
keep rain chances around through mid-week, especially across 
southern portions of the area.

The front will be south of the region on Monday and remain 
there through mid week. Confidence is not the highest pertaining
to all aspects of sensible weather, namely precipitation. How 
far south that front sags will be a big factor in how much rain 
we see through the week. The farther south it stalls, the less 
likely our region will see continued rain chances through the 
mid week period. Guidance this afternoon continues to indicate 
the front may try to lift briefly northward as a warm front on 
Tuesday, which looks to feature the highest rain chances through
mid-week. PoPs currently range from around 50% across far 
northern NJ to around 80% across portions of southeastern PA, 
far southern NJ, and most of Delmarva. For Wednesday into 
Thursday, the front should again be on the move southward, 
lessening rain chances across the area. 

Regardless of exact frontal placement or rain chances, the 
entire area will be on the cool side of the boundary. Therefore,
confidence is high that temperatures will be below normal. In 
fact, temperatures will likely struggle to get out of the 60s 
areawide through most of this week. 


KEY MESSAGE 3...A closed mid-level low ejecting from the Ohio 
Valley is expected to lead to the development of a surface low 
off the Eastern Seaboard during the middle and latter parts of 
this week. Depending on the track of the low, it could bring 
increased rainfall chances to the region. 

Model guidance this afternoon continues to indicate that a mid-
level low will track eastward out of the Ohio Valley region 
towards the Mid-Atlantic by Thursday. From there, it may become 
cutoff and meander off the Eastern Seaboard into late this week 
and potentially even into this weekend. As the mid-level low 
tracks eastward, surface cyclogensis will become favored off the
coast of the Carolinas. This could begin as early as Tuesday 
night as synoptic- scale ascent increases. The surface low is 
then likely to track northeastward into late this week. 

There is considerable uncertainty in how close the low will 
track to our area, and therefore, what impacts it may bring. 
Most guidance features a track well offshore, but the 
deterministic ECMWF and GFS continue to feature a westward 
deviation of the low late this week, which would lead to 
increased rain chances across the region. However, when looking 
at their ensemble members, the deterministic runs actually lie 
on the western edge of the overall envelope. 

All this being said, the forecast for the latter half of this 
week into this weekend features considerable uncertainty. For 
now, have PoPs generally in the 20-40% range across the eastern 
two-thirds of the area Friday through Sunday. However, if a 
westward deviation of the low does occur these could certainly 
trend up, or if the low remains farther out to sea the region 
could be mostly dry for the latter part of the week.


KEY MESSAGE 4...Multiple rounds of tidal flooding are expected
later this week, with tidal flooding potentially beginning as
early as Tuesday evening. 

Regardless of the exact track of the coastal low, it looks as 
if we will be in persistent onshore flow from at least Tuesday 
onward for the Atlantic Coast, Delaware Bay, and Raritan Bay. 
This long of an onshore flow component increases the risk for 
tidal flooding, especially for back bays. For the later half of 
the week, the track, strength of the low, and fetch will all 
play a role with tidal departures. In addition, the full moon is
on Saturday, meaning astronomical high tides are increasing as 
we get towards the end of the week.

Minor tidal flooding could begin as early as Tuesday
afternoon/evening's high tide with potential Moderate tidal
flooding on Wednesday. 

For the Chesapeake Bay, the expected wind direction tends to
limit tidal flooding concerns, but it will need to be watched if
persistent easterly flow at the mouth of the Chesapeake.
